If you are not aware by now, Buckstone is planning a construction of a new quarry site on Verdon Road in the historic Knoll area. I come to you tonight to specifically speak to the proposal of the quarry as many of my comments that are specific matter addressed later in the meeting. I come tonight asking you all to look at the bigger picture when considering development of the county.

While industrial revenue stimulates our local economy, all too often the residents and visitors feel the negative effects. As our county continues to grow, our infrastructure, emergency spots, and services need to grow accordingly. When proposals for large projects are considered, you need to consider what burdens they will place on the residents and county services.

While growth may bring additional revenue to additional services, it should not come at the expense of destroying the rural areas many taxpaying citizens enjoy in the county. I have noticed a trend in Hanover County of building massive warehouses and manufacturing facilities.

Route 1 is slowly becoming a line of concrete walls where one small business has stood. The infrastructure of rural Hanover County cannot support the additional heavy vehicle traffic associated with these types of businesses. The roads are narrow with no shoulders, limited areas to reroute, and our bus routes are for school-aged children.

Furthermore, the roads are often the last roads to be cleared of snow and ice and receive no sand or salt treatment. This creates additional hazards that lead to the long-lasting effects on the environment, safety, and well-being of the residents. Industrial manufacturing facilities will cause major increase of the use of aquifers that many of our residents use for their homes and farming through drilled wells.

As we found out earlier this year, and as of recent last week, the county cannot currently support the demand for those already in the system without the help from Richmond, never mind expanding it. When industrial manufacturing facilities move into our backyard, so do hazardous materials for the products they produce and use.

The chemicals include oxidizers, corrosives, poisons, carcinogens, explosives, and many more. All of these carry their own specific hazards and effects. These type of chemicals and facilities require specific types of training and response from our emergency services to mitigate safety and reduce its impact on its environment.
